latin: quae unitatem in trinitatem disponit, tres dirigens patrem et filium et spiritum, tres autem non statu, sed gradu, nec substantia, sed forma, nec potestate, sed specie, unius autem substantiae et unius status et unius potestatis, quia unus deus, ex quo et gradus isti et formae et species in nomine patris et filii et spiritus sancti deputantur. <qui> quomodo numerum sine diuisione patiuntur, procedentes tractatus demonstrabunt.

english: which distributes the Unity into a Trinity, placing in their order the three Persons— the Father, the Son, and the Holy Ghost: three, however, not in condition, but in degree; not in substance, but in form; not in power, but in aspect; yet of one substance, and of one condition, and of one power, inasmuch as He is one God, from whom these degrees and forms and aspects are reckoned, under the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: The economy distributes the one unity into a Trinity of three persons, three by degree, form and aspect, not by substance, power or condition.
use: supports Trinitarian reading: one substance, one power, three persons in the economy.
limits: "Gradus", "forma" and "species" are the words subordinationists quote; Tertullian says they do not divide the one substance.

latin: quale est, ut deus diuisionem et dispersionem pati uideatur in filio et in spiritu sancto, secundum et tertium sortitis locum, tam consortibus substantiae patris, quas non patitur in tot angelorum numero, et quidem tam <alienorum> a substantia patris?
latin_edition: Q. Septimi Florentis Tertulliani Adversus Praxean, ed. E. Kroymann (Tubingen: J. C. B. Mohr, 1907); Google scan on archive.org (item tertullianadver00tertgoog), read as page images at 130-260 dpi; image-only PDF, no text layer, so pdftotext cannot confirm pages; read on printed p. 4 (PDF 34)
english: how comes it to pass that God should be thought to suffer division and severance in the Son and in the Holy Ghost, who have the second and the third places assigned to them, and who are so closely joined with the Father in His substance, when He suffers no such (division and severance) in the multitude of so many angels?
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: Praxeas's ideas would make God divided, if the Son and Spirit, who share the Father's substance, are given second and third places.
use: answer to objection: the "second and third places" argument against Son and Spirit.
limits: The consortes are said to be of the Father's substance; the objection (second and third = lesser) is answered only by the argument from the monarchy. Latin consortes is the word the "consortium" search asked for.

latin: secundus autem ubi est, duo sunt, et tertius ubi est, tres sunt. tertius enim est spiritus a deo et filio, sicut tertius a radice fructus ex frutice et tertius a fonte riuus ex flumine et tertius a sole apex ex radio. nihil tamen a matrice alienatur, a qua proprietates suas ducit. ita trinitas per consertos et connexos gradus a patre decurrens et monarchiae nihil obstrepit et oikonomiae statum protegit.
latin_edition: Q. Septimi Florentis Tertulliani Adversus Praxean, ed. E. Kroymann (Tubingen: J. C. B. Mohr, 1907); Google scan on archive.org (item tertullianadver00tertgoog), read as page images at 130-260 dpi; image-only PDF, no text layer, so pdftotext cannot confirm pages; read on printed p. 11 (PDF 41)
english: Now the Spirit indeed is third from God and the Son; just as the fruit of the tree is third from the root, or as the stream out of the river is third from the fountain, or as the apex of the ray is third from the sun. Nothing, however, is alien from that original source whence it derives its own properties. In like manner the Trinity, flowing down from the Father through intertwined and connected steps, does not at all disturb the Monarchy, while it at the same time guards the state of the Economy.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: The Spirit is third from God and the Son in the economy, as fruit is third from the root, and the Trinity is a connected order of degrees.
use: supports Trinitarian reading: explicit "tres sunt" with the Spirit as third; the Latin "trinitas" is named in the sentence.
limits: Anti-Trinitarians read "tertius" and the tree/river/ray images as emanation or derivation (the Spirit as a product). Tertullian uses it of the economy, not of substance.

latin: sic alium a se paracletum, quomodo et nos a patre alium filium, ut tertium gradum ostenderet in paracleto, sicut nos secundum in filio propter oikonomiae

english: thus making the Paraclete distinct from Himself, even as we say that the Son is also distinct from the Father; so that He showed a third degree in the Paraclete, as we believe the second degree is in the Son, by reason of the order observed in the Economy.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: The Paraclete is distinct from the Father as the Son is, and shows a "third degree" as the Son shows a "second", by the order of the economy.
use: supports Trinitarian reading: "tertium gradum" for the Spirit, in the economic order; Tertullian says this is distinction, not diversity (9.1).
limits: "Alium ... alium" is the anti-Trinitarian proof text for three different beings; the "gradus" language is open to a subordinate reading.

latin: immo, quia iam adhaerebat illi [filius] secunda persona, sermo ipsius, et tertia, spiritus in sermone, ideo pluraliter pronuntiauit: 'faciamus' et 'nostram' et 'nobis'. cum quibus enim faciebat hominem et quibus faciebat similem? - filio quidem, qui erat induturus hominem, spiritu uero, qui erat sanctificaturus hominem - quasi cum ministris et arbitris ex unitate trinitatis loquebatur.
latin_edition: Q. Septimi Florentis Tertulliani Adversus Praxean, ed. E. Kroymann (Tubingen: J. C. B. english: Nay, it was because He had already His Son close at His side, as a second Person, His own Word, and a third Person also, the Spirit in the Word, that He purposely adopted the plural phrase, Let us make; and, in our image; and, become as one of us. For with whom did He make man? And to whom did He make him like? (The answer must be), the Son on the one hand, who was one day to put on human nature; and the Spirit on the other, who was to sanctify man. With these did He then speak, in the Unity of the Trinity, as with His ministers and witnesses.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: The plural in Gen 1:26 is spoken to the Son (second person) and the Spirit (third person) "in the unity of the Trinity".
use: supports Trinitarian reading: Spirit as "tertia persona" with the Son, from Gen 1:26.
limits: "Persona" here is the economic person (Word, Spirit in the Word); opponents read it as Word and Power, not distinct persons.

latin: absit. nos enim, qui et tempora et causas scripturarum per dei gratiam inspicimus, maxime paracleti, non hominum discipuli, duos quidem definimus, patrem et filium, et iam tres cum spiritu sancto, - secundum rationem oikonomiae quae facit numerum, ne, ut uestra peruersitas infert, pater ipse credatur natus et passus, quod non licet credi, quoniam non ita traditum est -
latin_edition: Q. Septimi Florentis Tertulliani Adversus Praxean, ed. E. Kroymann (Tubingen: J. C. B. english: For we, who by the grace of God possess an insight into both the times and the occasions of the Sacred Writings, especially we who are followers of the Paraclete, not of human teachers, do indeed definitively declare that Two Beings are God, the Father and the Son, and, with the addition of the Holy Spirit, even Three, according to the principle of the divine economy, which introduces number, in order that the Father may not, as you perversely infer, be Himself believed to have been born and to have suffered,
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: Tertullian says the followers of the Paraclete define two beings as God (Father and Son) and "even three" with the Holy Spirit, by the economy that makes the number.
use: supports Trinitarian reading: explicit count "et iam tres cum spiritu sancto".
limits: He adds "secundum rationem oikonomiae" and that the Father is not born or suffering; anti-Trinitarians read "duos ... tres" as numbers of beings, not one substance.

latin: dicens autem 'spiritus dei', etsi spiritus dei **, tamen non directo deum nominans, portionem totius intellegi uoluit, quae cessura erat in filii nomen. hic spiritus dei idem erit sermo.

english: Now, by saying the Spirit of God (although the Spirit of God is God,) and by not directly naming God, he wished that portion of the whole Godhead to be understood, which was about to retire into the designation of the Son.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)

use: explanation of hard passage: Tertullian explains the Spirit of God as a portion of the Godhead, not the whole.
limits: Anti-Trinitarians use "portio" and "non directo deum" to say the Spirit is not God; Tertullian says the Spirit is God in 26.6 but as a portion.

latin: et ideo spiritus deus et sermo deus, quia ex deo, non tamen ipse, ex quo est. quod<si> deus dei tamquam, substantiua res, non erit ipse deus, sed hactenus deus, qua ex ipsius dei substantia [quae et substantiua res est] et ut portio aliqua totius, multo magis uirtus altissimi non erit ipse altissimus, quia nec substantiua res est, quod est spiritus, sicut nec sapientia, nec prouidentia.
latin_edition: Q. Septimi Florentis Tertulliani Adversus Praxean, ed. E. Kroymann (Tubingen: J. C. B. Mohr, 1907); Google scan on archive.org (item tertullianadver00tertgoog), read as page images at 130-260 dpi; image-only PDF, no text layer, so pdftotext cannot confirm pages; read on printed p. 43 (PDF 73), with a crop at 260 dpi. DISCREPANCY: scan reads "quod<si> deus dei", Latin Library reads "quodsi spiritus dei"
english: And thus the Spirit is God, and the Word is God, because proceeding from God, but yet is not actually the very same as He from whom He proceeds. Now that which is God of God, although He is an actually existing thing, yet He cannot be God Himself (exclusively), but so far God as He is of the same substance as God Himself, and as being an actually existing thing, and as a portion of the Whole. Much more will the power of the Highest not be the Highest Himself, because It is not an actually existing thing, as being Spirit — in the same way as the wisdom (of God) and the providence (of God) is not God: these attributes are not substances, but the accidents of the particular substance. Power is incidental to the Spirit, but cannot itself be the Spirit.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: The Spirit is God and the Word is God because they proceed from God, but the Spirit is not the Father and is God only as a portion of his substance.
use: supports Trinitarian reading for the "Deus of the Spirit" question (Spirit is God, since from God), with the qualification of the Spirit being a portion.
limits: Holmes qualifies "God" as "so far God"; the phrase "non tamen ipse" and "portio" are cited against the full divinity of the Spirit; the scan/Latin Library discrepancy must be checked on the print edition.

limits: Only the Father-Son distinction; no statement about the Spirit.

latin: ita et spiritus dei, ut pati possit in filio, quia non in patre pateretur, sed in filio, pater passus non uideretur. sed sufficit nihil spiritum dei passum suo nomine, quia, si quid passus est in filio

english: So likewise the Spirit of God, whatever suffering it might be capable of in the Son, yet, inasmuch as it could not suffer in the Father, the fountain of the Godhead, but only in the Son, it evidently could not have suffered, as the Father. But it is enough for me that the Spirit of God suffered nothing as the Spirit of God, since all that It suffered It suffered in the Son.
translator: Peter Holmes (ANF vol. 3, ed. Roberts/Donaldson/Coxe; revised for New Advent by Kevin Knight)
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: The Spirit of God could suffer only in the Son, not in the Father, and as the Spirit it suffered nothing.
use: answer to objection: the Father or Spirit suffered on the cross; Tertullian keeps the Spirit distinct from the Son, as a fountain-river image.
limits: Opponents read "spiritus dei passum" as a distinct being who could suffer; Tertullian denies the Spirit suffered as Spirit.

latin: Quamquam etsi omnem hanc persecutionem condicionalem in solos tunc apostolos destinasset, utique per illos cum toto sacramento, cum propagine nominis, cum traduce spiritus sancti in nos quoque spectasset etiam persecutionis obeundae disciplina ut in hereditarios discipulos et apostolici seminis frutices.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text; no print edition named on the page; not checked against a print edition or scan
english: Though, even if He had appointed all this persecution in case He were obeyed for those only who were then apostles, assuredly through them along with the entire sacrament, with the shoot of the name, with the layer of the Holy Spirit, the rule about enduring persecution also would have had respect to us too, as to disciples by inheritance, and, (as it were,) bushes from the apostolic seed.
translator: Rev. S. Thelwall (ANF)
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 1413 (English, Chapter IX); Latin page unknown
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: The persecution rule is given through the apostles with the sacrament, the name and the "traducem" (line) of the Holy Spirit, extending to later disciples.
use: context: the Holy Spirit is the transmission (traducem) of the apostolic line; Trinitarian reading is indirect.
limits: Nothing about the Trinity here; "traduce" is a figure for transmission, so it is weak evidence for the Trinity.

latin: necesse erat portionem spiritus sancti quae ex forma prophetici moduli in Ioanne egerat praeparaturam viarum dominicarum, abscedere iam ab Ioanne, redactam scilicet in dominum ut in massalem suam summam.
latin_edition: thelatinlibrary.com text; no print edition named on the page; not checked against a print edition or scan
english: Now, that the very Lord Himself of all might, the Word and Spirit of the Father, was operating and preaching on earth, it was necessary that the portion of the Holy Spirit which, in the form of the prophetic gift, had been through John preparing the ways of the Lord, should now depart from John, and return back again of course to the Lord, as to its all-embracing original.
translator: Holmes (ANF vol. 3; the volume note at PDF 795 refers to "Dr. Holmes" as translator of this work; not confirmed on the page of this passage)
page: ANF vol. 3 p. 806 (English); Latin page unknown
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 3 (Buffalo: Christian Literature Pub. Co., 1885) PDF on archive.org, text layer; printed page from page footer
what_it_says: The portion of the Holy Spirit that worked in John the Baptist returned to the Lord, who is its whole source.
use: context: the "portio" language for the Holy Spirit; this is about Marcion's Christ, not the Trinity.
limits: Book 3 and most of Book 4 were searched for Spirit, trinitas and tertium gradum; Adv. Marc. 3 has no Spirit passage, and the Holy Spirit appears only in 4.18 and 4.26 (as a gift of the demiurge). This is a negative result for the brief's "3.6 and 4" request.
